newsitem.title: USA: NYCE cotton closes down slightly, volume light.
newsitem.headline: NYCE cotton closes down slightly, volume light.

text.p: NYCE cotton futures closed slightly weaker after a lackluster and thinly-traded session, dealers said.
Prices managed to hold above the contract lows hit across the board on Tuesday, amid scattered buying by the trade, they added.

Most-active July ended 0.10 cent lower at 71.92 cents per lb, having ranged from 72.10 to 71.65 cents. December finished down 0.17 cent to 74.46 cents, while the rest of the board finished unchanged to 0.26 cent lower.
Technical support in July was seen at the contract low of 71.00 cents hit Tuesday, and then at 70.00 cents.
Volume was estimated at 5,000 lots compared with Tuesday's official 16,806 lots.

Floor sources said several players took to the sidelines after two consecutive sessions in which active July fell to a new life-of-contract low, and ahead of the first official supply and demand estimates for the 1997/98 crop.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture will issue its report on Monday at 0830 EDT.
Analysts said that while the market will trade on Monday's production estimate, the number could come in substantially higher than actual output.

The estimate is based on the USDA's March planting intentions estimate of 14.4 million acres, but planted area is expected to decline due to weather-induced planting delays across the cotton belt, high soybean prices, and weak new-crop December prices.
"I'm surprised that December is so lackluster given the potential for less acreage planted in 1997," Carl Anderson, a cotton marketing specialst with Texas A & M University, said.

He said the flat tone that has been maintained for several weeks may indicate that stocks are adequate. "We've reached a status quo as far as supply and demand, and the market is trading along without any particular fundamental or technical news changing that," Anderson said.

Market analysts agree that a rise in polyester consumption is partly to blame. They point to the April consumption report, which fell far below expectations, and cited a growing production capacity for polyester in the Far East.
Concern over certificated stocks and supplies in the CCC loan program, continues to weigh on the market. Stocks remained steady at 220,870 bales, as of May 6, NYCE said.
